I am a Ph.D. student at Rice University, working in Prof. Taiyun Chi’s lab. I design analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits for neural interfaces, ultrasonic sensing, and electrochemical readout. My work covers circuit design, chip fabrication, and measurement.

01 / SELECTED RESEARCH

Biomedical circuits and
design automation.

My research focuses on integrated circuits for biomedical sensing. I work on neural recording and stimulation, ultrasonic sensing, and electrochemical readout, where the circuits must resolve small signals while keeping noise, power, and size low. I am also interested in developing AI-based methods for analog and mixed-signal circuit design that can be applied across different applications.

01 / NEURAL INTERFACESRice University · 2024–Present

Scaling neural recording
and stimulation.

Recording activity across many neurons can help researchers understand how neural circuits control movement and how they respond to stimulation. Increasing the number of channels, however, places tighter limits on the power and area available to each channel while the circuits must still resolve weak neural signals. For this project, we developed a chip with 512 recording channels and 128 stimulation channels for spinal cord research and the development of approaches to restore movement after injury.

4 µVrmsinput-referred noise · 10 kHz BW
20 µWper recording channel
±10 Vstimulation compliance
Design contributions & validation

Led the recording-chip architecture and analog circuit design, focusing on capturing weak neural signals with low noise and power consumption. Contributed to the stimulation circuitry, tested the fabricated chip, and participated in in vivo validation.

TSMC 180 nm BCD · Silicon validated
02 / NEURAL INTERFACES · BIOPOTENTIAL AMPLIFIERSRice University · 2025

Compact, low-noise amplifiers
for scalable neural recording.

As neural interfaces grow to thousands of recording sites, each amplifier must detect microvolt-level signals while occupying little area and consuming little power. In advanced CMOS, leakage currents can shift the amplifier’s operating point, while internal DC offsets can produce ripple during chopping. These effects can limit the stability and noise performance of a compact amplifier. Building on the neural-interface work above, we developed an amplifier that addresses these challenges through leakage compensation, internal offset cancellation, and a gate-body-driven input stage.

2.35 µVrmsinput-referred noise · 10 kHz bandwidth
2.1 µWpower consumption
0.0195 mm²amplifier area
Design contributions & validation

Developed an amplifier architecture that compensates leakage from the pseudo-resistor and input transistors and uses controlled pseudo-resistor leakage to cancel internal DC offset. The gate-body-driven input stage improves noise efficiency without additional power or area overhead. Measurements in 22-nm CMOS SOI showed that the first-stage differential output offset decreased from approximately 400 mV to 0.2 mV, and integrated input-referred noise decreased by 15%. In a phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) setup, recordings of prerecorded neural signals closely matched those obtained with an Intan RHD2164 system (R² = 0.99).

Manuscript under review · IEEE TCAS II
03 / ULTRASONIC SENSINGRice University · 2021–2023

Ultrasonic through-transmission for non-invasive intracranial pressure sensing.

Intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring helps clinicians assess patients with brain injuries and other neurological conditions. Conventional methods require placing a sensor inside the skull, limiting where and how monitoring can be performed. Changes in ICP also cause small changes in skull dimensions, which can be detected by measuring how long ultrasound takes to travel across the head.

In this work, we developed a through-transmission ultrasonic transceiver for non-invasive ICP sensing. Two transducers placed on opposite sides of the head measure changes in ultrasound time of flight. The direct signal arrives before internal reflections, and operating at a constant frequency avoids frequency-dependent phase errors associated with variable-frequency approaches. The transceiver consumes less than 9 mW, and its time-to-digital converter provides sub-µm displacement resolution.

Sub-µmTDC displacement resolution
<9 mWpower consumption
Design contributions & validation

Designed the ultrasonic transmitter, receiver, and time-of-flight measurement circuitry. The time-to-digital converter has a timing resolution of 29.8 ps, corresponding to 45.9 nm of displacement at an assumed ultrasound speed of 1,540 m/s. In a head-phantom experiment, the measured displacement waveform correlated with a reference ICP sensor (R² = 0.92).

ISSCC 2024 · IEEE TBioCAS 2024
04 / ELECTROCHEMICAL SENSINGimec · 2023–2024

Scalable electrochemical readout
for sensing neural chemistry.

Electrochemical sensors provide information about chemical activity by measuring small currents or changes in voltage at an electrode. Reading many sensors at once requires circuits that can resolve these signals within a limited area and power budget. At imec, we developed a current-mode delta-sigma readout for redox and pH sensing. A shared potentiostat reduces the circuitry required for each channel, while direct current digitization simplifies the readout. To reduce low-frequency noise from the feedback current DAC, we introduced an autozeroing technique.

12.6 pArmsamperometric noise · 10 mHz–10 Hz
0.0055 mm²per amperometric channel, including shared potentiostat
0.016 pHISFET pH resolution
Design contributions & validation

Developed an autozeroing technique for the feedback current DAC to reduce flicker noise and mismatch between the source and sink currents. The collaborative 130-nm CMOS prototype includes 16 amperometric channels and an ISFET readout channel. Measurements showed 12.6 pA rms amperometric noise from 10 mHz to 10 Hz and a combined 100 dB dynamic range across programmable current ranges. In vitro experiments demonstrated redox sensing and an ISFET pH resolution of 0.016 pH.

VLSI 2026 · Collaborative work at imec
